bull.argument: Apple's filing shows a business growing strongly and returning substantial capital. Total net sales rose 15% to $478,834 million in 2026 from $416,161 million, with iPhone up 21% and Services up 13% to $123,301 million. Greater China grew 28%, and total gross margin percentage expanded to 48.8% from 46.9%. Operating leverage is visible too: total gross margin rose to $233,602 million while operating expenses grew 22%, and the Company still holds $136.9 billion in cash, cash equivalents and marketable securities. Management also returned $85.8 billion through buybacks and $15.7 billion in dividends, and announced a new $100 billion repurchase program. The filing does flag real risks: supply constraints, rising memory costs, tariffs, and a warning that gross margins will see 'volatility and downward pressure.' But the Company has already passed higher costs through pricing and mix, and it reports tariff refunds from the Supreme Court ruling. A business with this scale, cash generation, and demonstrated pricing power deserves a strong investment case despite those headwinds.

claims.claim: Total net sales grew 15% year over year in 2026.
Gross margin percentage expanded, showing the business is converting growth into profit.
Management returned large amounts of capital and announced a new buyback.
claims.quote: In April 2026, the Company announced a new share repurchase program of up to $100 billion

bear.argument: The bull case leans on 2026 results that the filing itself qualifies. Gross margin expansion was driven partly by tariff refunds, which are non-recurring: the Company's own text says tariffs may be rescinded and refunds are uncertain. Management also states that it 'believes, in general, gross margins will be subject to volatility and downward pressure,' and that supply constraints and rising costs for memory and storage 'expects these trends to intensify.' Price increases 'may also reduce demand.' Operating expenses rose 22%, with R&D up 32% on AI infrastructure, a spend whose returns the filing says 'may not achieve expected returns.' Greater China's 28% jump came after a 4% decline a year earlier, and the Company faces 'aggressive price competition' and a minority share in its core markets. Cash of $136.9 billion is offset by $78.7 billion of notes and $89.7 billion of manufacturing purchase obligations.

claims.claim: Management expects gross margins to face downward pressure, despite the 2026 expansion.
claims.quote: the Company believes, in general, gross margins will be subject to volatility and downward pressure

claims.claim: Part of the 2026 margin gain came from tariff refunds that may not recur.
claims.quote: If tariffs are subsequently rescinded or revoked, the Company may not be able to successfully claim and collect tariff refunds.

claims.claim: Heavy AI-related R&D spending may not earn its expected returns.
claims.quote: These investments may not achieve expected returns, and the Company may not be able to develop and market new products, services and technologies successfully.

bull.argument: The opponent is right that several 2026 figures are flattered by one-time or volatile factors, and I should concede that plainly. Tariff refunds did help Products gross margin, and the filing says the Company may not collect refunds if tariffs are rescinded. But the core trend does not rest on refunds alone. Services gross margin percentage rose to 76.2% from 75.4%, and Services net sales grew 13% to $123,301 million, a stream that is largely recurring. Total net sales grew 15%, with iPhone up 21%, so the top line is not just a refund story. Greater China's rebound from a 4% decline is a recovery, not a flat trend, and it is still a 28% gain. On the opponent's point about cash: $136.9 billion in cash and securities against $78.7 billion of notes means the Company is not leaning on debt to fund its $85.8 billion of buybacks. The filing's warnings about margins and AI returns are real, and they justify a position sized for volatility rather than a straight-line bet.

claims.claim: Services revenue grew 13%, a more recurring income stream than hardware.
Services gross margin percentage rose, showing mix improvement beyond refunds.
Cash and securities exceed the Company's notes outstanding.
claims.quote: the Company had outstanding fixed-rate notes with varying maturities for an aggregate principal amount of $78.7 billion

bear.argument: The bull case still leans on numbers the filing itself qualifies. Services gross margin percentage rose to 76.2%, but the Company attributes that to 'a different mix of services,' not a durable rate change, and its own outlook says gross margins will see 'volatility and downward pressure.' Products margin rose to 39.3% partly on tariff refunds, which the filing says may not be collectible if tariffs are rescinded. Calling the top line 'not just a refund story' overlooks that iPhone growth came from 'higher net sales of Pro models,' while iPad and Wearables were flat and Wearables fell 4% the prior year. Management also expects memory and storage cost pressure to 'intensify,' and the Company says price increases 'may also reduce demand.' On cash, $136.9 billion is real, but $89.7 billion of manufacturing purchase obligations, $82.7 billion due within 12 months, is a near-term claim on that cash. Buybacks of $85.8 billion, against $15.7 billion of dividends, are a large capital outflow the filing does not tie to any cash-flow guarantee.

claims.claim: Management attributes the Services margin gain to product mix and expects margins to face downward pressure.
claims.quote: the Company believes, in general, gross margins will be subject to volatility and downward pressure

claims.claim: Products margin gains were partly driven by tariff refunds that may not be collected if tariffs are rescinded.
claims.quote: If tariffs are subsequently rescinded or revoked, the Company may not be able to successfully claim and collect tariff refunds.

claims.claim: Near-term manufacturing commitments are large relative to cash on hand.
claims.quote: As of September 26, 2026, the Company had manufacturing purchase obligations of $89.7 billion, with $82.7 billion payable within 12 months.

judge.reasoning: Both sides cite verified quotes, but the bear's quotes directly target the bull's weakest points: refund-flattered margins, downward margin guidance, and near-term obligations. The bull conceded the refund issue but leaned on Services and cash comparisons, where its cash-vs-notes argument ignored the $82.7 billion of obligations due within 12 months that the bear raised. The bear's responsiveness is somewhat stronger, though the bull's concession and Services-mix rebuttal were reasonable.
